items.title: Kings Rumors: Acuff, Sabonis, LaVine, Kuminga, More
items.content:
Shortly after the Kings landed the No. 7 pick in the 2026 draft lottery, rumors of their interest in former Arkansas guard Darius Acuff Jr. began to percolate. That chatter turned out not to be a smoke screen. As Anthony Slater of ESPN writes, Acuff was “definitely” ranked higher than seventh on Sacramento’s draft board and was considered the team’s “dream scenario” outside of one of the consensus top four prospects (AJ Dybantsa, Darryn Peterson, Cameron Boozer, and Caleb Wilson).

While there were some rumblings leading up to draft night that the Clippers and Nets might consider Acuff with the fifth and sixth overall picks, respectively, general manager Scott Perry remained confident that the Kings’ top target would fall to them and didn’t feel compelled to move up. His restraint was rewarded, and Acuff – who heard all the same rumors about Sacramento’s desire to draft him – is eager to reward the franchise for its belief in him.

“I heard the noise (about how much they wanted me),” Acuff told ESPN at Summer League. “I wanted to be a part of this team and this organization.”

As Slater writes, the coming season figures to be a year of transition for the Kings, who are building around Acuff and their young core while veterans like Domantas Sabonis and Zach LaVine remain on the roster. Sabonis and LaVine are taking a positive approach and trying to make the best of the situation, according to Slater, who hears that both players reached out to Acuff shortly after he was drafted to convey their enthusiasm about teaming up with him.

“An excellent gesture,” Perry said. “It’s important that the veterans that are around not only can show or offer constructive criticism or constructive feedback to a young player like him. It’s also incumbent upon them to encourage, welcome and help fast-track his growth as well too in this particular situation.”

Here’s more from Slater on the Kings:

Perry met with Sabonis for two hours shortly after being hired by the Kings in 2025 and the two men have had an open line of communication since then, with the front office sharing potential trade scenarios involving the big man, Slater writes. After trade talks with the Raptors, Pistons, Hornets, and Celtics didn’t ultimately result in a deal at the 2026 deadline or earlier this offseason, Sabonis has expressed that he’s committed to this season’s Kings team, per Slater, who says the three-time All-Star traveled to Las Vegas for Summer League and met with Perry again in Sacramento last week to discuss the future.
Although Sabonis is eligible for an extension this offseason with two years left on his current contract, a new deal isn’t something the team is currently exploring, Slater says, noting that the veteran center recently changed agents, signing with CAA Sports. items.title: Jalen Pickett, Clippers Agree To Two-Way Deal
items.content:
The Clippers and free agent guard Jalen Pickett have reached an agreement on a two-way contract, league sources tell Michael Scotto of HoopsHype (Twitter link).

Pickett, 26, spent the past three seasons in Denver after being selected with the 32nd overall pick in the 2023 draft. The former Penn State standout barely played as a rookie, but he took on more of a rotation role over the past couple years. In 2025/26, he appeared in 50 games, making 18 starts, and averaged 5.2 points, 2.3 assists, and 2.3 rebounds in 16.1 minutes per night.

Pickett has shown some ability to space the floor. After knocking down 38.1% of his outside shots in his final college season, the 6’2″ guard has converted 38.7% at the NBA level, averaging 5.7 three-point attempts per 36 minutes.

The Nuggets held a $2.4MM team option on Pickett for the 2026/27 season, which would have cost slightly less than a veteran’s minimum deal. However, the cap-strapped club decided not to pick up that option and then didn’t tender Pickett a qualifying offer, allowing him to become an unrestricted free agent. Now, he appears set to fill the lone two-way opening on the Clippers’ roster alongside Sean Pedulla and 2026 second-rounder Nick Martinelli.

Big man Jamarion Sharp was also reported to have a two-way deal in place with L.A. a couple weeks ago, but that agreement has yet to be officially finalized. Assuming the team still intends to add Sharp along with Pickett, Pedulla may be the odd man out — his two-way contract carried over from last season, whereas Martinelli just signed his in July.

Pickett will earn up to $678,882 on his two-way contract and will be eligible to appear in as many as 50 regular season games. The deal will cover one season, putting him on track for free agency again in 2027.

items.title: 2027 NBA Trade Deadline Set For Feb. 11
items.content:
The NBA’s trade deadline for the 2026/27 season will land on Thursday, February 11 at 3:00 pm Eastern time, according to the league’s official list of key upcoming dates (hat tip to Yossi Gozlan of The Third Apron).

With the exception of the 2020/21 NBA league year, which started later than usual due to COVID, this season will have the latest trade deadline since 2016/17. That was the last year in which the deadline fell during the Thursday after the All-Star Game instead of two Thursdays before it.

The Feb. 11 deadline is worth highlighting at this time due to how it will affect players who sign veteran contract extensions for the rest of the 2026/27 league year. When a player signs a veteran extension, he may become ineligible to be traded for six months if his new deal meets certain criteria.

That means any player who signs a veteran extension between now and next Tuesday (August 11) will be trade-eligible at this season’s deadline, regardless of whether or not the six-month restriction applies to him. But any player who signs a veteran extension after next Tuesday will be ineligible to be traded this season if his new deal meets any of the following criteria:

His current contract and new extension exceed four years in total.
His starting salary on the extension is worth more than 120% of the final-year salary on his current deal (or 120% of the NBA’s estimated average salary, for a player earning below the average).
His salary increases or decreases by an amount greater than 5% between the first and second years of the extension (or in any subsequent seasons).
His current contract is renegotiated as part of the extension.

Celtics big man Neemias Queta is an example of a recently extended player who meets one or more of these criteria. He’s now under contract for five years in total and will get 8% annual raises on his new contract with Boston. That means Queta is ineligible to be traded for six months, but because his deal was finalized on July 6, his trade restrictions will lift on January 6, well before this season’s deadline.

This six-month restriction doesn’t apply to players who sign rookie scale extensions. They can be traded immediately, though the poison pill provision might make it difficult to do so.

Players who sign veteran extensions that don’t meet any of the criteria above are also eligible to be traded immediately. Another Celtic, forward Jordan Walsh, is one player who falls into this category. The three-year extension he signed last month resulted in him being under contract for four years in total; additionally, his new deal starts below the NBA’s estimated average salary and features 5% annual raises. As a result, no trade restrictions currently apply to Walsh.

November 11 is another date worth keeping in mind now that the trade deadline for 2027 is officially set. A free agent who signs with an NBA team after Nov. 11 won’t become trade-eligible this season

items.title: Atlantic Notes: Brown, Wagner, Nets, Martin
items.content:
Publicly addressing the Sixers‘ signing of LeBron James for the first time during a Twitch stream on Monday, Jaylen Brown expressed excitement about the prospect of teaming up with one of the NBA’s all-time greats, as James Jackson of The Athletic relays.

“What an opportunity that is,” Brown said. “Like, obviously, everybody (is) gonna say whatever they want to say, and it’s gonna be a bunch of media this whole entire season. But, for me, what an opportunity (it) is to learn. I love learning, so to have the opportunity to learn from one of, if not the greatest player of all time.”

Brown also said on the live stream that being traded from Boston to Philadelphia has him feeling more motivated than ever to win, adding that he has lost some weight this summer in anticipation of doing more running in transition alongside his new teammates.

“Just to be a little bit more fast and nimble,” Brown said. “I gotta keep up with (Tyrese) Maxey and (VJ) Edgecombe and LeBron this year, so I did lose about seven pounds. I feel great. I’m jumping higher, running faster.”

We have more from around the Atlantic:

Moritz Wagner‘s new two-year contract with the Nets, originally reported to be worth $19MM, ended up coming in a little lower than that, according to Keith Smith of Spotrac, who tweets that Wagner will earn exactly $9MM in 2026/27, with a second-year mutual option worth $9.45MM. In total, the deal is worth $18.45MM, leaving Brooklyn with about $4.9MM in remaining cap room.
Confirming that the pending divorce between Nets owners Joe Tsai and Clara Wu Tsai won’t impact the team’s basketball or business operations in any way, Brian Lewis of The New York Post (subscription required) takes a closer look at the ownership situation in Brooklyn. A spokesperson for Brooklyn Sports & Entertainment, the holding company that controls the Nets and the WNBA’s New York Liberty, tells Lewis that the Tsais – who have previously referred to the Nets as a “family business” – plan to eventually involve their children in the management of the franchise.
The two-year, minimum-salary contract that Alijah Martin signed with the Raptors last month is fully guaranteed in year one and includes a $500K partial guarantee in year two, tweets Blake Murphy of Sportsnet.ca. Martin will receive his full $2.57MM salary for 2027/28 if he remains under contract through July 1, 2027.

items.title: Hoops Rumors Glossary: Exhibit 9 Contract
items.content:
When NBA teams are in the process of filling out their training camp rosters, the Exhibit 10 is the type of contract mentioned most frequently on Hoops Rumors. An Exhibit 10 contract can be converted into a two-way deal or puts a player in line to earn a bonus if he’s waived and then joins his team’s G League affiliate.

While we spend more time talking about Exhibit 10 deals, most of those non-guaranteed training camp contracts also include an Exhibit 9 clause in addition to – or in place of – Exhibit 10 language.

An Exhibit 9 clause protects an NBA team in the event that a player suffers a significant injury in training camp.

If a player on a standard non-guaranteed contract without an Exhibit 9 clause suffered such an injury, his club would be required to pay him his salary until he’s healthy enough to play or until the end of that season, whichever comes first. For example, a player on a non-guaranteed rookie minimum deal who sustained a season-ending ACL tear would be owed his full $1,357,763 salary.

If the injured player’s contract includes Exhibit 9 language, however, his team could waive him and only be on the hook for a one-time payment of $15K. That amount increased from $6K when the NBA and NBPA completed its latest Collective Bargaining Agreement.

An Exhibit 9 deal, which is non-guaranteed and doesn’t count against the salary cap until the start of the regular season, can only be a one-year, minimum-salary contract. A team can carry up to six players on Exhibit 9 deals, but can’t sign a player to such a contract unless it has at least 14 players already under contract (not including two-way deals).

In most cases, if a team plans to have a player on a non-guaranteed contract participate in training camp and/or the preseason, his contract will include an Exhibit 9 clause in order to limit the club’s liability.

If a player signs a contract that includes Exhibit 10 language but not an Exhibit 9 clause, it’s usually a signal that he’s just being added for G League rights/bonus purposes and won’t actually be participating in training camp with his team. Conversely, an Exhibit 9 contract that doesn’t include Exhibit 10 language suggests the player will probably be taking part in camp but may not be a candidate to join his team’s G League affiliate if he’s waived.

So far this offseason, eight players have signed Exhibit 10 contracts, and all eight of those deals include an Exhibit 9 clause as well. Meanwhile, four players – including three Pelicans (Christian Koloko, Kobe Bufkin, and Caleb Houstan) – have signed Exhibit 9 contracts that do not feature Exhibit 10 language.

An Exhibit 9 contract that also includes Exhibit 10 language can be converted into a two-way deal. In that scenario, the Exhibit 9 clause would become null and void, so the team would no longer have injury protection.

items.title: Early NBA Maximum Salary Projections For 2027/28
items.content:
Although a number of big-money free agent contracts were completed earlier this summer, the two most lucrative deals signed by players so far in 2026/27 have been contract extensions. Both of those extensions have been maximum-salary deals.

[RELATED: 2026/27 NBA Contract Extension Tracker]

Because those extensions won’t go into effect until the 2027/28 season and the NBA won’t finalize its ’27/28 salary cap until next summer, we can only ballpark what many of year’s maximum-salary contracts will look like based on the league’s latest cap estimates.

The NBA’s most recent projection for ’27/28 called for a cap of $174MM, which is the number we’ll use to project next season’s maximum salaries.

Listed below are the early maximum-salary projections for 2027/28. The first chart shows the maximum salaries for a player re-signing with his own team — a player’s previous club can offer five years instead of four, and 8% annual raises instead of 5% raises. The second chart shows the maximum salaries for a player signing with a new team.

A player’s maximum salary is generally determined by his years of NBA experience, so there’s a wide gap between potential earnings for younger and older players. Unless they qualify for a more lucrative extension by meeting certain performance criteria, players with no more than six years of NBA experience are limited to a starting salary worth up to 25% of the cap. For players with seven to nine years of experience, that number is 30%. For players with 10 or more years of experience, it’s 35%.

Wembanyama could have added “Rose rule” language to his extension, making him eligible for a starting salary worth 30% of the cap if he earns an All-NBA spot in 2027, but he opted not to do so. items.title: Nuggets Hire Dave Joerger As Assistant Coach
items.content:
August 5: The Nuggets have officially hired Joerger as an assistant coach, they confirmed today in a press release.

Appearing this week on DNVR Sports’ Nuggets podcast, Stein said he has heard there was a mandate from management for Adelman to add an assistant with head coaching experience this offseason, which is what led the team to Joerger (Twitter video link).

July 27: The Nuggets will hire Dave Joerger to be the top assistant coach under head coach David Adelman, according to Shams Charania of ESPN (via Twitter).

Marc Stein reported a couple weeks ago that Denver was viewed as an “increasingly likely” landing spot for Joerger, who has been an NBA assistant or head coach since 2007. Joerger interviewed in June for the lead assistant position, as Stein previously reported.

Joerger also drew interest from Australia’s Melbourne United and the EuroLeague team Paris Basketball, but he decided to stay in the NBA in an assistant role rather than making the move overseas.

The 52-year-old spent several years as an assistant in Memphis before being promoted to the Grizzlies’ head coach in the 2013 offseason. He compiled a 147-99 record (.598 win-loss percentage) in three years as Memphis’ top coach, making the playoffs on each occasion, before being let go in May 2016.

Joerger was quickly hired by Sacramento and spent the next three seasons as the Kings’ head coach, going 98-148 (.398) before being dismissed in 2019. He has spent the past several years as an assistant in Philadelphia and — most recently — Milwaukee.

The Nuggets have been looking for an experienced No. 2 coach under Adelman, a longtime assistant who took over as Denver’s head coach when Michael Malone was fired near the end of the 2024/25 season. The Nuggets went 54-28 in ’25/26 and entered the playoffs as the third seed in the Western Conference, but were eliminated in the first round by Minnesota.

items.title: Sixers Officially Sign Kentavious Caldwell-Pope
items.content:
The Sixers have made it official with Kentavious Caldwell-Pope, announcing today in a press release that they’ve signed the veteran wing to a contract.

It was first reported nearly two weeks ago that Caldwell-Pope was being bought out by Memphis and would sign with Philadelphia after clearing waivers. The 33-year-old gave up $3,876,529 in his buyout agreement with the Grizzlies, which is the exact amount he’ll earn on his new one-year, minimum-salary deal with the 76ers. The team will carry a cap hit of $2,449,421.

A two-time NBA champion with the Lakers and Nuggets, Caldwell-Pope established himself as a reliable three-and-D option during his prime years, averaging 10.7 points per game and making 40.3% of his three-point attempts in 365 regular season outings during a five-season stretch from 2019-24.

That run earned Caldwell-Pope a three-year, $66MM deal from the Magic as a free agent in 2024, but he struggled during his lone season in Orlando before being traded to Memphis as part of the Desmond Bane blockbuster during the 2025 offseason. The 13-year veteran had another down year with the Grizzlies and was no longer considered part of the rebuilding club’s plans going forward, so Memphis was happy to negotiate a buyout that helped alleviate its roster crunch.

The Sixers are optimistic about Caldwell-Pope’s ability to bounce back in 2026/27 as a role player on a star-studded squad that includes fellow Rich Paul clients LeBron James, Tyrese Maxey, Justin Edwards, and Jabari Walker in addition to former MVP Joel Embiid, All-NBA second-teamer Jaylen Brown, and Rookie of the Year finalist VJ Edgecombe.

In order to fit Caldwell-Pope’s minimum-salary contract below their second-apron hard cap, the 76ers traded Johni Broome to the Clippers last week along with a second-round pick. Philadelphia now has roughly $1.8MM in breathing room below that hard cap, with 14 players on standard contracts.

While the Sixers can’t add a 15th man on a veteran’s minimum deal until December based on their current cap situation, it’s worth noting that Walker’s salary is only partially guaranteed for $250K. It sounds like the club would prefer to hang onto the veteran forward, but if an opportunity arises to add another coveted minimum-salary target, waiving Walker would create enough room below the first apron to make it happen.

items.title: Rockets Waive JD Davison
items.content:
The Rockets have waived guard JD Davison, the team announced today.

Houston picked up its 2026/27 team option on Davison in June, but his $2,584,539 salary remained entirely non-guaranteed even after that option was exercised. As a result, the Rockets won’t carry any dead money on their cap for Davison, whether or not he’s claimed on waivers.

Davison, the 53rd overall pick in the 2022 draft, spent his first three NBA seasons on two-way contracts with the Celtics but appeared in just 36 total regular season games for Boston, averaging 5.5 minutes per contest.

Davison saw a bit more action in 2025/26 on a two-way deal with the Rockets, but still played just 7.8 MPG in 28 outings, averaging 2.5 points, 1.3 assists, and 1.2 rebounds per game on .375/.250/.684 shooting. The 23-year-old was promoted to the standard roster prior to the postseason and saw garbage-time action in a pair of playoff games.

The former Alabama guard has made a far more significant impact in the G League, particularly in 2024/25, when he earned G League MVP honors with the Maine Celtics. In 45 total NBAGL appearances that season, he averaged 25.6 points, 7.7 assists, 5.1 rebounds and 1.4 steals in 34.6 minutes per game.

As a result of waiving Davison, the Rockets have moved below the luxury tax line by a mere $14,077, tweets Yossi Gozlan of The Third Apron. It’s likely no coincidence that that’s the exact amount that a player on a prorated minimum-salary contract would earn for a single day in service.

In other words, even if Houston doesn’t shed any additional salary between now and the end of the regular season, the club would be able to sign a player to a minimum contract prior to the regular season finale without going into luxury tax territory.

The Rockets’ 14 players on standard contracts include 12 on fully guaranteed deals, one (Jae’Sean Tate) on a partially guaranteed contract, and one (Isaiah Crawford) who has a non-guaranteed salary. Crawford would earn a partial guarantee if he’s still under contract to open the regular season, but if a training camp invitee such as Oscar Tshiebwe or Julian Phillips outperforms him in the preseason, Houston could swap in one of those players for Crawford without altering its cap situation.

items.title: Celtics Sign Dillon Mitchell To Two-Way Deal
items.content:
The Celtics have signed rookie forward Dillon Mitchell to a two-way contract, the team announced on Wednesday (Twitter link).

The extremely athletic 6’8″ forward was the 40th pick in the 2026 draft and proceeded to average 13.0 points, 2.7 steals, and 1.3 blocks in 26.0 minutes per game for the Celtics in Summer League while hitting 37.5% of his limited three-point attempts.

A defensive standout who earned a spot on the Big East’s All-Defensive team as a senior, Mitchell never averaged more than 9.9 points per game in any of his four college seasons, so it remains to be seen how much he’ll contribute offensively at the NBA level.

Still, the Celtics have had success with similar types of players in recent years, including the recently extended Jordan Walsh and 2025 rookie Hugo Gonzalez, who had an impressive start to his NBA career last season.

One of the few remaining unsigned rookies, Mitchell was reported to be considering a return to St. John’s after a federal court ruling granted him and other seniors from his class a fifth year of eligibility. However, that preliminary injunction doesn’t apply to players who have signed professional contracts, so this two-way deal suggests Mitchell is committed to beginning his NBA career.

Mitchell is now the second two-way player under contract for the Celtics, alongside big man Amari Williams.

items.title: Heat Notes: LaVine, Targets, Spoelstra, Johnson
items.content:
The Heat‘s desire to add a high-volume shooter to replace the recently departed Tyler Herro and Norman Powell and bolster their offense around the talented duo of Bam Adebayo and Giannis Antetokounmpo is no secret, nor is their scant means of acquiring said player.

There was hope that the matter could be neatly resolved if the Kings decided to buy out or waive-and-stretch Zach LaVine, a high-level floor-spacing guard who has one year and $49MM remaining on his deal. However, Sacramento is reportedly uninterested in going down that route at the moment.

Miami can only offer about $8MM from its mid-level exception, and it’s unlikely that LaVine giving up that amount would move the needle for the Kings, whereas if Klay Thompson gave up a similar amount on his smaller expiring deal, it could hold more appeal for the Mavericks, Ira Winderman writes for the South Florida Sun Sentinel.

The Kings are also not facing any kind of financial hardship that would make them desperate to get off LaVine’s deal before it expires next season, Anthony Chiang notes for the Miami Herald. Ultimately, any possibility of LaVine joining the Heat could come down to how much the 31-year-old would be willing to sacrifice to facilitate the move.

We have more from the Heat:

While the odds are against LaVine heading to South Beach, the Heat still need to fill at least two roster spots with a little over $10MM in wiggle room below the first apron. Bradley Beal, DeMar DeRozan, and Thompson are three potential targets they’ve been frequently linked to, prompting Chiang to weigh each player’s pros and cons. Beal’s health remains a question mark – he hasn’t appeared in 60+ games since the 2020/21 season – but he can play either guard spot and reliably knock down outside shots. DeRozan remains productive despite being on the threshold of turning 37, but he would not bring the three-point shooting the team so badly needs. As for Thompson, he’s still a high-level shooter, but he struggles with contributing in other areas at this point and isn’t currently a free agent like Beal and DeRozan.
The Heat’s moves this summer have generated both intense excitement and some skepticism, depending on who you talk to. While the defense has the potential to be one of the best in the league, there are real questions about how the offense will function with limited ball-handlers and shooters. Still, one key reason for optimism has been largely overlooked, Winderman writes: Erik Spoelstra‘s elite coaching ability. Spoelstra has accomplished great things with far less impressive rosters in the past, and has proven himself more than capable of adjusting his approach to fit his personnel. He has also been one of the better coaches in the league at empowering unheralded players and turning them into contributors on winning teams, which will be a crucial aspect of this team’s ability to regain its foothold as a true tit

items.title: Suns, Dillon Brooks Agree To Three-Year Extension
items.content:
The Suns have agreed to sign veteran forward Dillon Brooks to a three-year contract extension worth $73MM, ESPN’s Shams Charania reports (via Twitter).

The contract is fully guaranteed and contains no options, per Suns insider John Gambadoro (Twitter link). The first year will start at just over $22MM.

Brooks had a career year as a scorer last season, his first with the club after coming over from the Rockets in the Kevin Durant trade. He averaged 20.2 points on 17.1 shots per game, both career highs, and helped establish a tough-minded mindset for a team looking to reestablish its culture following Durant’s departure.

Phoenix exceeded expectations after revamping its roster during the 2025 offseason, finishing seventh in the Western Conference before being swept out of the first round of the playoffs by the Thunder. Brooks’ ability to step up and be the secondary scoring option on the team while stabilizing the wing depth as Jalen Green battled health issues was a crucial part of that success.

Acknowledging that there’s a chance the deal “might approach overpay territory” before it expires, Gerald Bourguet of Suns After Dark (Twitter link) notes that the Suns value Brooks’ off-court leadership and culture-setting as much as anything he does on the floor.

The deal amounts to around 13% of the salary cap, according to Yossi Gozlan of the Third Apron (Twitter link), who believes it should retain positive trade value going forward. Because he’ll officially sign before August 11, Brooks will be eligible to be moved at the February 11 trade deadline if the team decides to go that route.

The Suns clearly valued continuity after overachieving last season, making it a priority to lock up several of their key contributors, Charania notes (via Twitter), with Collin Gillespie, Mark Williams, and Jordan Goodwin each signing new deals as free agents. This extension further solidifies those efforts, keeping Brooks under contract through the 2029/30 season.

items.title: Clippers To Waive Sean Pedulla
items.content:
The Clippers are waiving point guard Sean Pedulla, Michael Scotto reports for HoopsHype (Twitter link). The 23-year-old was on a two-way deal that he signed in February.

Pedulla played seven games for the Clippers last season, making 5-of-15 field goal attempts for 13 points in 31 total minutes. He spent the majority of his time with the team’s G League affiliate, the San Diego Clippers, after starting the season with the Rip City Remix, the Trail Blazers’ affiliate.

Pedulla was named G League Rookie of the Year after averaging 23.6 points, 6.7 assists, 5.0 rebounds and 1.6 steals in 28 total games between the Remix and the San Diego Clippers.

Pedulla was one of two Clippers two-way players, alongside this year’s 55th overall pick, Nick Martinelli. L.A. has reportedly agreed to two-way deals with Jamarion Sharp and Jalen Pickett, necessitating a roster move, since teams only have three two-way slots apiece.

items.title: Nuggets, Lonnie Walker IV Agree To One-Year Deal
items.content:
The Nuggets have agreed to a one-year deal worth $3.3MM with free agent wing Lonnie Walker IV, Shams Charania reports for ESPN (via Twitter). It’ll be a minimum-salary contract for Walker, who will earn $3,286,399 while Denver takes on a cap hit of $2,449,421.

Walker is an athletic, 6’4″ shooting guard who will help bolster Denver’s backcourt depth after they lost Tim Hardaway Jr. and Jalen Pickett this summer.

The 27-year-old out of the University of Miami played for Maccabi Tel Aviv last season, his first full year out of the league since being drafted 18th overall by the Spurs in 2018. He averaged 15.2 points per game on .394/.351/.758 shooting splits in EuroLeague play for the Israeli club.

Over his last five seasons in the NBA, Walker averaged 11.3 points in 22.4 minutes per night while shooting 35.2% from deep. He most recently played 20 games for the Sixers during the 2024/25 season, averaging a career-high 12.4 points per game.

It’s unclear if Walker’s deal with the Nuggets will be fully guaranteed, but if they envision him being part of their regular season roster, it likely spells the end of Bruce Brown‘s time in Denver. The team, which already has 13 players on standard guaranteed contracts prior to officially signing Walker, is still looking to resolve Peyton Watson‘s restricted free agency negotiations as well.

items.title: Why Draymond Green Didn’t Push For No-Trade Clause
items.content:
After declining his $27.7MM player option to give the Warriors a chance at landing a big-name free agent, which ultimately did not come to fruition, Draymond Green recently signed a one-year deal worth the same amount.

Green was eligible to receive a no-trade clause in this deal, as the rule stipulates a player must have spent at least four years with their current team, be signing a new deal rather than an extension, and have at least eight seasons of experience, but no such provision was forthcoming from Golden State.

In addition to the no-trade clause he was eligible for, Green could also have received an implicit no-trade clause, since he was signing a one-year deal, but he waived that right as well, instead receiving a 15 percent trade kicker, as he had in his previous deal, per ESPN’s Anthony Slater (Twitter link).

He spoke about the decision on a recent episode of his podcast, explaining his mindset coming out of the negotiations.

“I think it was something that we could have fought over, but it wasn’t worth fighting over,” he said (video link). “I think if the Warriors want to trade me at some point in the season, they want to trade me. I’ve never been a guy who wants to stay somewhere where I’m not wanted.”

With limited assets at the team’s disposal, Green’s name occasionally appeared in trade rumors this season, which is something of a rare occurrence throughout his tenure with the Warriors. He was open about the business angle of such possibilities throughout the process, but there has also always been reported interest from both sides in having Green finish his career in the Bay Area.

“I think there is a partnership that this works for us, it works,” Green said. “If it doesn’t, it doesn’t, you know, and I never want to be that guy anyway. So, to sit and fight over a no-trade clause, I don’t think it was worth it. It’s pointless. So, that wasn’t a thing.”

Only one player will have a no-trade clause entering the 2026/27 season: Damian Lillard, who negotiated one into his deal last summer.
